hypothesis: What happens to cyclists, drivers, local shops and the public budget if the Bloor St W bike lane between Shaw St and Avenue Rd is removed under Bill 212?
retrieval_query: bike lane removal parking business retail cycling diversion safety Toronto Bloor

selected_claims.paper_title: Bloor Street West Bike Lane Pilot Project Evaluation
selected_claims.source_location: pages 7, 10-11 (cycling, vehicle volume and travel time tables)
selected_claims.finding: After installation, Bloor cycling rose from 3,309 to 4,925 per day, about 25% of the increase was new riders and the rest rerouted from Harbord and Dupont; Bloor vehicles fell 16% with net three-corridor change of -3%; peak travel times rose 0:32 to 4:15.
selected_claims.method: municipal before/after counts and GPS travel-time runs
selected_claims.setting: Bloor St W, Shaw St to Avenue Rd, June 2016 to June 2017
selected_claims.transfer_warning: Installation effects; a 2026 removal may not reverse them one-for-one.

selected_claims.paper_title: Bloor Street West Bike Lane Pilot Project Evaluation
selected_claims.source_location: pages 12-15 (parking table 5, economic impact findings, Moneris analysis)
selected_claims.finding: On-street parking fell from 303 to 167 spaces (total paid spaces -10%); paid parkers -5.95%; point-of-sale value grew 4.45% in the pilot area vs 3.73% surrounding, 2.21% Danforth and 4.96% city-wide; 90% of visitors arrived without a car.
selected_claims.method: Toronto Parking Authority monitoring, aggregated Moneris transactions, intercept surveys
selected_claims.transfer_warning: Aggregate spending trend, not shop-level sales; growth trailed the city-wide trend.

selected_claims.paper_title: Bike Lanes, On-Street Parking and Business: Year 2 Report
selected_claims.finding: 21% of Bloor West Village visitors usually drove, yet 69% of merchants believed more than 20% of customers drove; 46% of merchants expected fewer customers with a bike lane.
selected_claims.setting: Bloor West Village, Toronto (Year 2 survey; report published 2010)
selected_claims.transfer_warning: Different street segment and population from the Annex; perceptions, not sales.

selected_claims.paper_title: Economic impacts on local businesses of investments in bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure: a review of the evidence
selected_claims.authors: Jamey M. B. Volker; Susan Handy
selected_claims.finding: Across 23 studies, active-travel facilities generally had positive or non-significant effects on retail and food service, but bicycle facilities may hurt auto-oriented businesses.
selected_claims.transfer_warning: Installation evidence; use for heterogeneity, not a removal coefficient.

selected_claims.paper_title: Vancouver Separated Bike Lane Business Impact Study
selected_claims.finding: Businesses on Hornby and Dunsmuir reported estimated sales declines of about 10% and 4% after separated lanes opened.
selected_claims.method: business, customer and employee surveys with comparison streets
selected_claims.transfer_warning: Perception-based with about one-third response and major confounders; primary PDF not checked.

conflicting_claims.resolution: Do not choose one retail coefficient. Run negative, zero and positive retail cases and keep the shop-response chain labelled assumption-driven.
Seed some merchant personas with an overestimated driving share and let survey evidence challenge it; Annex merchants in 2008 estimated more accurately (B05).
Treat reversal of 2016-2017 effects as a sensitivity case, including partial reversal and a construction-disruption period (B11).

required_next_step: Retrieve an actual human note and source passage from Papiers for B01 or B04, ask a human to choose/edit/reject the proposed reversal and retail cases, then version and rerun.
